title: Designing a Workflow Repository
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of designing a workflow repository and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to designing a workflow repository.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on designing a workflow repository. A workflow repository should make CI, security, deployment, custom actions, reusable workflows, and configuration ownership easy to discover and review. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Designing a Workflow Repository matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A workflow repository should make CI, security, deployment, custom actions, reusable workflows, and configuration ownership easy to discover and review. A professional pipeline is evidenced, not merely diagrammed: document decisions, prove success and selected failure paths, trace artifacts to commits, and review security and recovery.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A workflow repository should make CI, security, deployment, custom actions, reusable workflows, and configuration ownership easy to discover and review. A professional pipeline is evidenced, not merely diagrammed: document decisions, prove success and selected failure paths, trace artifacts to commits, and review security and recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Separating CI, security, and deployment workflows
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Organizing custom actions

items.title: Documenting secrets and variables
items.text: Store credentials in the appropriate protected secret store, pass them only to the step that needs them, and never print or save them in logs, summaries, artifacts, or caches.

items.title: Establishing naming and versioning conventions
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

name: Controlled workflow review
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Review permissions, triggers, artifacts, and recovery evidence"
content_blocks.expected_output: The manually started job prints a checklist reminder; a real review must validate the actual workflow and retain reviewed evidence.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to designing a workflow repository. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain designing a workflow repository, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Plan, validate, document, and present a production-ready automation system.

content.task: Apply designing a workflow repository to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A workflow repository should make CI, security, deployment, custom actions, reusable workflows, and configuration ownership easy to discover and review.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A workflow repository should make CI, security, deployment, custom actions, reusable workflows, and configuration ownership easy to discover and review. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: A workflow repository should make CI, security, deployment, custom actions, reusable workflows, and configuration ownership easy to discover and review.
A professional pipeline is evidenced, not merely diagrammed: document decisions, prove success and selected failure paths, trace artifacts to commits, and review security and recovery.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
